In individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) can be utilized on sputum samples for the initial detection of resistance to isoniazid and fluoroquinolones. This approach is recommended over culture-based phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence regarding diagnostic accuracy. 2. For individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance, low-complexity automated NAATs may be used on sputum samples to initially detect resistance to ethionamide. This is preferred over DNA sequencing of the inhA promoter. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for diagnostic accuracy. 3. In cases of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB with rifampicin resistance, low-complexity automated NAATs may also be employed on sputum samples for the initial detection of resistance to amikacin, rather than relying on culture-based phenotypic DST. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for diagnostic accuracy. 4. For individuals with a sputum smear-positive specimen or a cultured isolate of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), commercial molecular line-probe assays (LPAs) may be used as the initial test to detect resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. This is recommended instead of phenotypic culture-based DST. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty in the evidence for the test’s accuracy. 5. For patients with confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), second-line line-probe assays (SL-LPAs) may be used as the initial test to detect resistance to fluoroquinolones. This is recommended over phenotypic culture-based DST. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence for test accuracy in direct sputum testing and low certainty for indirect testing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures. 6. Similarly, for patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB, SL-LPAs may be used as the initial test to detect resistance to second-line injectable drugs, rather than phenotypic culture-based DST. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for direct sputum testing and very low certainty for indirect testing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures. 7. In individuals with bacteriologically confirmed TB, high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs may be used on Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture isolates to detect pyrazinamide resistance. This is recommended over culture-based phenotypic DST. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for diagnostic accuracy. 8. Commercial serodiagnostic tests should not be used in children suspected of having active pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, regardless of their HIV status. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for the use of commercial serodiagnostics. 9. In children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB (without suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB), a 4-month treatment regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) is recommended over the standard 6-month regimen. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 10. Non-severe TB is defined as peripheral lymph node TB, intrathoracic lymph node TB without airway obstruction, uncomplicated TB pleural effusion, or paucibacillary, non-cavitary disease confined to one lobe of the lungs without a miliary pattern. 11. Children and adolescents who do not meet the criteria for non-severe TB should receive the standard 6-month treatment regimen (2HRZE/4HR) or the recommended treatment regimens for severe forms of extrapulmonary TB. 12. Evidence from the SHINE trial (Shorter Treatment for Minimal Tuberculosis in Children) demonstrated that a 4-month treatment regimen is non-inferior to the standard 6-month regimen for children with non-severe, drug-susceptible TB. This trial was a multi-center, open-label, randomized, controlled, non-inferiority trial. 13. The SHINE trial included children under 16 years of age treated with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, with or without ethambutol, using WHO-recommended pediatric dosing. The trial enrolled 1,204 children between July 2016 and July 2018, with a median age of 5 years, 52% male, 11% HIV-infected, and 14% bacteriologically confirmed TB. 14. The primary efficacy outcome of the SHINE trial was a composite of treatment failure, on-treatment loss-to-follow-up, TB recurrence, or death by 72 weeks. The non-inferiority margin was set at 6%. 15. The trial found no significant difference in adverse events between the 4-month and 6-month treatment arms. Most adverse events were related to pneumonia or other chest infections and liver-related events. 16. The SHINE trial results support the use of a 4-month regimen for children with non-severe TB, as it demonstrated non-inferiority in treatment outcomes compared to the 6-month regimen. 17. The shorter treatment regimen is associated with potential benefits, including reduced costs for families and health systems, lower toxicity, fewer drug-drug interactions in children living with HIV, and improved adherence. 18. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) emphasized the importance of clearly defining non-severe TB and scaling up access to quality chest X-rays (CXR) and training for healthcare providers in interpreting CXRs to ensure accurate classification of disease severity. 19. Subgroup analyses in the SHINE trial showed no difference in outcomes between the 4-month and 6-month regimens for children with peripheral lymph node TB or those with both peripheral lymph node and pulmonary disease. 20. For children and adolescents living with HIV (CALHIV), clinicians may consider a 4-month treatment regimen for non-severe TB, depending on the degree of immunosuppression, antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, and the presence of other opportunistic infections. Close monitoring is required, especially at 4 months, with treatment extension to 6 months if progress is insufficient. 21. Children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) were included in the SHINE trial, but no separate subgroup analysis was conducted for this population.
